what_its_for: Cefoxitin is an antibiotic used to treat or prevent certain bacterial infections. It can be used for infections of the skin, lungs, urinary tract, stomach, bones, joints, and reproductive organs. It is also sometimes given before surgery to help prevent infection.
how_to_take: Cefoxitin is given as an injection or IV (intravenous) infusion directly into a vein. You will receive this medicine in a hospital, clinic, or infusion center. A trained healthcare provider will give you each dose. You will not inject this medicine yourself at home unless specifically instructed and trained by your healthcare team. Each infusion usually takes about 15 to 30 minutes.
dosing: Your doctor will decide your dose based on your type of infection, your weight, kidney function, and overall health. Adults typically receive 1 to 2 grams every 6 to 8 hours, but doses may be higher for serious infections. Children's doses are based on body weight. Always follow your doctor's exact dosing schedule and complete the full course of treatment, even if you feel better.
missed_dose: Because cefoxitin is given by a healthcare provider in a medical setting, it is unlikely that you will miss a dose. However, if you miss a scheduled appointment or infusion session, contact your doctor or care team right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not try to double up doses on your own.
storage: Cefoxitin will be stored and prepared by your healthcare team. If you are given any supplies to use at home, keep them in a cool, dry place away from light and heat. Refrigerate any mixed (prepared) solutions as directed, usually between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze the mixed solution. Always check the expiration date and throw away any unused medicine properly.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as cefoxitin can interact with other drugs. Avoid drinking alcohol during your treatment. Do not take any new over-the-counter medicines, especially blood thinners or pain relievers like ibuprofen, without asking your doctor first. Do not skip doses or stop treatment early, as this can allow the infection to come back or become harder to treat.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency help right away if you experience: a severe allergic reaction (trouble breathing, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, hives, or dizziness); severe diarrhea or stomach cramps that are watery or bloody (this could be a serious bowel infection called C. diff); skin rash, blistering, or peeling; yellowing of the skin or eyes; dark urine or unusual fatigue; pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site; seizures; or any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within a few days of starting cefoxitin. However, it is very important to complete your full course of treatment as prescribed by your doctor, even if your symptoms improve. Stopping too early can allow the infection to return or become resistant to antibiotics.
special_populations: Kidney problems: Your doctor will adjust your dose if your kidneys do not work well. Make sure to tell your doctor about any kidney disease before starting treatment. Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Cefoxitin may be used during pregnancy if clearly needed and the benefits outweigh the risks. Breastfeeding: Small amounts of cefoxitin may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Cefoxitin can be used in children, including newborns, but the dose will be carefully calculated by your doctor based on weight and age. Elderly: Older adults may need a lower dose due to reduced kidney function. Your doctor will monitor you closely.
